# 1. Operational Cost Baseline for the Region

This profile synthesises current intelligence on fuel-cost drivers for freight-forwarding operations. It is written for workspaces whose primary transport mode is air, with road as secondary and ocean tertiary, moving high-value and time-sensitive cargo across US and international lanes. The sourced content is a US national and global crude-benchmark dataset rather than a single sub-national jurisdiction: US Gulf Coast, New York Harbor, and Los Angeles spot markets, plus the WTI (Cushing, Oklahoma) and Brent (Europe) crude benchmarks.

### COST ALERT

**Jet fuel, US Gulf Coast (air-primary mode).**

FACT: the EIA's daily series records US Gulf Coast kerosene-type jet fuel spot prices, "U.S. Gulf Coast 3.987 3.392 3.253 3.304 3.237 3.569 1990-2026" *Source: EIA Spot Prices for Crude Oil and Petroleum Products, US Energy Information Administration. https://eia.gov/dnav/pet/pet_pri_spt_s1_d.htm

*Operational implication:* the range across this series, roughly 3.253 to 3.987 dollars per gallon, signals that aviation fuel surcharges built on weekly or monthly averages can lag actual spot exposure by a material margin. For workspaces operating on air as the primary mode across transatlantic or transpacific lanes, this range creates fuel-surcharge timing risk, since carriers buy fuel at daily spot while surcharge pass-through mechanisms typically clear on a delay.

**Crude oil benchmarks.**

FACT: "WTI - Cushing, Oklahoma 100.35 97.63 92.35 92.65 91.16 95.96 1986-2026" *Source: EIA Spot Prices. https://eia.gov/dnav/pet/pet_pri_spt_s1_d.htm

FACT: "Brent - Europe 106.90 102.75 97.11 95.47 92.88 98.29 1987-2026" *Source: EIA Spot Prices. https://eia.gov/dnav/pet/pet_pri_spt_s1_d.htm

*Analytical inference:* the WTI-Brent spread implied by the latest values in these two series is narrower than historical norms. "June 2023" is when WTI Midland was integrated into the Brent basket, reducing the traditional structural discount that landlocked Cushing delivery imposed. For workspaces pricing fuel on Brent-linked carrier surcharges on European lanes, this narrowed spread reduces the historical surcharge arbitrage between US-origin and Europe-origin shipments.

FACT: "75%" *Source: ICE Insights, "What are the differences between ICE Brent and NYMEX WTI Futures?" https://www.ice.com/insights/energy/what-are-the-differences-between-ice-brent-and-nymex-wti-futures

*Analytical inference:* workspaces operating on European and Asian trade lanes will find that carrier fuel surcharges on those routes are predominantly Brent-indexed, given how widely Brent is used as the reference benchmark per the figure above.

**EIA STEO forecast versus recent spot.**

FACT: "The Brent crude oil spot price increased sharply in April , reaching a high of $138 per barrel (b) on April 7 and averaging $117/b for the month, as the de facto closure of the Strait of Hormuz tightened global oil supplies." *Source: EIA Short-Term Energy Outlook. https://www.eia.gov/outlooks/steo/

FACT: "we expect crude oil prices to fall, dropping to an average of $89/b in 4Q26 and $79/b in 2027." *Source: EIA Short-Term Energy Outlook. https://www.eia.gov/outlooks/steo/

FACT: "We expect global oil inventories will fall by an average of 8.5 million b/d in the second quarter of 2026 (2Q26), keeping Brent prices around $106/b in May and June." *Source: EIA Short-Term Energy Outlook. https://www.eia.gov/outlooks/steo/

*Analytical inference:* the gap between the April spike and current spot levels represents genuine cost relief compared to mid-crisis pricing, but the forecast full-year annual average remains elevated relative to the prior year, meaning year-on-year fuel-cost comparison benchmarks stay significantly elevated for any workspace using a prior-year actual as its budget reference.

# 6. Client Conversation Talking Points

**What the workspace can credibly say:**

- Jet fuel spot prices have fallen significantly from the April peak. Brent peaked sharply in April and is currently trading well below that peak, per the sourced STEO commentary and daily spot data (Section 1). The workspace can accurately describe a material decline from the crisis peak when discussing current fuel surcharge trajectories with clients.
- The forward curve suggests further moderation is priced in by the market for the out-years, though this reflects current market expectations, not a guarantee.
- The current elevated prices reflect a specific geopolitical event (the Strait of Hormuz disruption), not a structural long-run supply shift; the EIA's own forecast projects prices declining as production recovers.

**Pitfalls to avoid:**

*Analytical inference:* do not claim that fuel surcharges will fall immediately or on a specific schedule; carrier surcharge mechanisms vary and are not sourced in this brief. Do not claim that the Strait of Hormuz is fully open: the captured EIA forecast states shipping traffic through the strait was assumed to remain constrained, with a slow recovery path, and no sourced date for full recovery is available in the captured source blocks. Do not claim that Brent and WTI prices are interchangeable for surcharge purposes; carriers use different benchmarks by route and mode.

**Pitfall: using the STEO forecast as current pricing.**

*Analytical inference:* the STEO forecast and the daily spot data are two different things; citing the forecast as current pricing overstates or understates fuel costs to clients depending on direction. Use the EIA daily spot data for current-state claims, and the STEO for directional medium-term framing only.

---

# 7. Pending Changes That Shift the Calculus

### MONITORING

**Monitoring timeline:**
- June 9, 2026: next EIA Short-Term Energy Outlook release, expected to revise the fuel-price forecast path.
- Jun 10, 2026: next EIA weekly spot-price data release.
- May 1, 2026: the UAE's departure from OPEC took effect, reducing forecast OPEC spare capacity.

FACT: "Updated: Jun 3, 2026 12:12 PM CDT Next Release Date: Jun 10, 2026" *Source: EIA Spot Prices page. https://eia.gov/dnav/pet/pet_pri_spt_s1_d.htm

*Analytical inference:* given that actual spot prices have diverged from the STEO's own assumed price path for the period it covers, the next STEO release will likely revise the annual average, which would shift the planning baseline for fuel-cost assumptions, SAF pricing models, and carrier surcharge projections.

FACT: "This report assumes that the Strait of Hormuz remains effectively closed until late May, with shipping traffic beginning to pick up in June. Oil shipments through the strait, however, will not likely reach pre-conflict levels until later this year" "Oil shipments through the strait, however, will not likely reach pre-conflict levels until later this year, and we expect some oil production in the Middle East to remain disrupted over that period." *Source: EIA Short-Term Energy Outlook. https://www.eia.gov/outlooks/steo/

*Analytical inference:* the pace of Strait of Hormuz recovery is a leading variable driving fuel-cost trajectory for the second half of 2026; workspaces with air-freight contracts renewing in the near term should monitor recovery pace as a trigger for renegotiating fuel-surcharge mechanisms. No sourced date for full recovery is available in the captured source blocks.

FACT: "We assess that Iraq, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, the UAE, Qatar, and Bahrain collectively shut in 10.5 million barrels per day (b/d) of crude oil production in April." *Source: EIA Short-Term Energy Outlook. https://www.eia.gov/outlooks/steo/

FACT: "The UAE announced its departure from OPEC, effective May 1, 2026. Our May STEO incorporates that change." *Source: EIA Short-Term Energy Outlook. https://www.eia.gov/outlooks/steo/

*Analytical inference:* the reduction in OPEC spare capacity following this departure structurally reduces the cartel's ability to buffer future supply shocks; for freight operations with significant Middle East routing or Gulf hub transshipment, this reduces the reliability of the historical OPEC-buffer assumption in carrier cost models.

FACT: "thermal units) $3.50 $3.18 Previous forecast $3.67 $3.59 Percentage change -4.4% -11.5% U.S. marketed natural gas p" *Source: EIA Short-Term Energy Outlook. https://www.eia.gov/outlooks/steo/

*Analytical inference:* for freight operations with warehouse or terminal energy costs tied to natural gas tariffs, this Henry Hub projection represents a modest cost relief relative to an earlier projection.

entries.body:
# 1. Operational Cost Baseline for the Region

This profile covers solar-plus-battery-energy-storage (BESS) system feasibility and the US federal tax-credit landscape for warehouse facilities. It is written for workspaces whose warehouse estate includes US-domiciled facilities, particularly those handling time-critical or climate-sensitive cargo (live events equipment, fine art, luxury goods, high-value automotive, humanitarian relief).

*Note:* the item's own primary source (an NREL commercial-storage case study) returned only a short interstitial in this capture pool; the substantive content is a US Department of Energy solar-and-storage explainer plus a US Treasury/IRS final-regulation Federal Register notice.

GAP: [cost_baseline] Specific industrial electricity rates, capex figures, or payback-period data for warehouse-scale solar-plus-BESS are not present in the captured source blocks; the NREL technical reports that would populate this baseline (REopt resilience valuation, optimal sizing studies) were identified as corroborating leads but not retrievable in this capture.

FACT: "AGENCY: Internal Revenue Service (IRS), Treasury. ACTION: Final regulations." Effective date: These regulations are effective on December 12, 2024. Applicability dates: For dates of applicability, see Sec. Sec. 1.48-9(g), 1.48-13(f), 1.48-14(j), and 1.6418-5(j). *Source: Federal Register, Definition of Energy Property and Rules Applicable to the Energy Credit, US Treasury / IRS final regulations. https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2024/12/12/2024-28190/definition-of-energy-property-and-rules-applicable-to-the-energy-credit

FACT: "The Treasury Department and the IRS confirm that energy storage technology is eligible for the section 48 credit if it satisfies the requirements of section 48 even if the energy storage technology is co-located with or shared by a facility that is otherwise eligible for the section 45, 45V, or 48 credits." *Source: Federal Register, US Treasury / IRS final regulations. https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2024/12/12/2024-28190/definition-of-energy-property-and-rules-applicable-to-the-energy-credit

*Analytical inference:* the confirmation that energy storage technology qualifies for the federal investment tax credit independent of co-location with a solar system establishes the US federal jurisdiction as the relevant tax-credit anchor for this profile; specific state or municipal jurisdiction figures (industrial electricity rates, local permitting costs) are not present in the captured source blocks.

FACT: "Solar and storage can provide backup power during an electrical disruption. They can keep critical facilities operating to ensure continuous essential services, like communications. Solar and storage can also be used for microgrids and smaller-scale applications, like mobile or portable power units." *Source: Solar Integration: Solar Energy and Storage Basics, US Department of Energy, 2024. https://www.energy.gov/cmei/systems/solar-integration-solar-energy-and-storage-basics

*Operational implication:* for warehouses holding high-value or time-sensitive freight, backup power continuity is a direct operational benefit beyond energy cost reduction; workspaces should evaluate solar-plus-storage against their insurance and service-level commitments for cargo that cannot tolerate temperature excursion or security-system failure during outages.

---

# 2. Feasibility of Specific Operational Choices

**Solar PV co-located with warehouse BESS, technically feasible.**

FACT: "Sometimes energy storage is co-located with, or placed next to, a solar energy system, and sometimes the storage system stands alone, but in either configuration, it can help more effectively integrate solar into the energy landscape." *Source: DOE Solar Integration explainer. https://www.energy.gov/cmei/systems/solar-integration-solar-energy-and-storage-basics

*Operational implication:* the DOE confirms both co-located and standalone storage as functional models; warehouse operators are not required to choose a single architecture, and the decision turns on roof area, load profile, and grid-interconnection terms rather than any technical prohibition.

**Electrochemical (lithium-ion) BESS, the dominant pairing with PV.**

FACT: "the storage technologies most frequently coupled with solar power plants are electrochemical storage (batteries) with PV plants and thermal storage (fluids) with CSP plants." "The most common chemistry for battery cells is lithium-ion, but other common options include lead-acid, sodium, and nickel-based batteries." *Source: DOE Solar Integration explainer. https://www.energy.gov/cmei/systems/solar-integration-solar-energy-and-storage-basics

**Short-term versus long-term storage, different operational roles.**

FACT: "Short-term storage that lasts just a few minutes will ensure a solar plant operates smoothly during output fluctuations due to passing clouds, while longer-term storage can help provide supply over days or weeks when solar energy production is low or during a major weather event, for example." *Source: DOE Solar Integration explainer. https://www.energy.gov/cmei/systems/solar-integration-solar-energy-and-storage-basics

*Operational implication:* for warehouse facilities handling time-critical cargo, the distinction between short-term and long-term BESS has direct operational relevance; short-term systems protect against intra-day solar variability, long-term systems address multi-day outage or grid-disruption scenarios.

**Pumped hydro, not feasible for warehouse application.**

FACT: "Pumped hydro is a well-tested and mature storage technology that has been used in the United States since 1929. However, it requires suitable landscapes and reservoirs, which may be natural lakes or man-made by constructing dams, requiring lengthy regulatory permits, long implementation times, and large initial capital." *Source: DOE Solar Integration explainer. https://www.energy.gov/cmei/systems/solar-integration-solar-energy-and-storage-basics

*Analytical inference:* the infrastructure requirements (reservoirs, dam construction, landscape suitability) are incompatible with commercial logistics facility footprints; this option is not worth pursuing for a freight forwarder's warehouse estate.

**Thermal storage, applicable only for concentrating-solar-adjacent configurations.**

FACT: "Thermal energy storage is a family of technologies in which a fluid, such as water or molten salt, or other material is used to store heat. This thermal storage material is then stored in an insulated tank until the energy is needed. The energy may be used directly for heating and cooling, or it can be used to generate electricity." *Source: DOE Solar Integration explainer. https://www.energy.gov/cmei/systems/solar-integration-solar-energy-and-storage-basics

*Analytical inference:* thermal storage is relevant for warehouse climate control (chilled or heated storage) but is not a primary electricity-generation storage path for standard logistics warehouse applications.

**Load-shifting value varies by grid mix and rate structure.**

FACT: "storage, which can be filled or charged when generation is high and power consumption is low, then dispensed when the load or demand is high." *Source: DOE Solar Integration explainer. https://www.energy.gov/cmei/systems/solar-integration-solar-energy-and-storage-basics

FACT: "Peak power usage often occurs on summer afternoons and evenings (link is external) , when solar energy generation is falling. Temperatures can be hottest during these times, and people who work daytime hours get home and begin using electricity to cool their homes, cook, and run appliances." *Source: DOE Solar Integration explainer. https://www.energy.gov/cmei/systems/solar-integration-solar-energy-and-storage-basics

*Analytical inference:* for workspaces with warehouse facilities across multiple regions, the financial return on solar-plus-BESS is not uniform; regions with time-of-use grid pricing or high peak-demand charges will show faster payback than regions with flat-rate or heavily subsidised grid power. Facilities in high-summer-temperature regions face the widest gap between peak solar generation and peak demand, so BESS sized to bridge that daily gap delivers the highest demand-charge reduction value there.

FACT: "Although using energy storage is never 100% efficient—some energy is always lost in converting energy and retrieving it—storage allows the flexible use of energy at different times from when it was generated." *Source: DOE Solar Integration explainer. https://www.energy.gov/cmei/systems/solar-integration-solar-energy-and-storage-basics

---

# 3. Cost Comparison Against Alternatives

*No content for this section as of 2026-09-17: the NREL technical reports that would carry payback and resilience-value figures for warehouse-scale solar-plus-BESS (REopt resilience valuation brochure, optimal sizing technical report) were identified as corroborating leads for this pass but were not retrievable in this capture pool.*

*No content for this section as of 2026-09-17: this record's stored pool is a general DOE explainer and a US federal tax-credit notice, not sourced figures for two or more of the workspace's active regions; no cross-regional footprint-allocation comparison can be proven from this single stored pool.*

---

# 5. Competitive Positioning in the Region

*No content for this section as of 2026-09-17: no named competitor's solar-plus-BESS deployment data for warehouse facilities is present in the captured source blocks.*

---

# 6. Client Conversation Talking Points

**What the workspace can credibly say:**

- Solar-plus-storage at warehouse facilities provides confirmed resilience benefits: backup power during grid disruption keeps critical cargo-storage environments operational. This is sourced from the US Department of Energy and is a supportable client statement.
- Lithium-ion BESS paired with rooftop or adjacent PV is the commercially dominant technology path for this application, not an emerging or experimental configuration.
- For clients with Scope 3 emissions reporting obligations, warehouse electricity sourced from on-site solar reduces the Scope 2 market-based emissions figure attributed to freight handling.

**Pitfalls to avoid:**

*Analytical inference:* do not cite specific payback periods, capex figures, or ROI percentages in client conversations unless drawn from a facility-specific engineering study; generic industry averages vary widely by region, utility rate structure, and roof configuration. Do not represent the US federal investment tax credit as automatically applicable to the workspace's warehouse portfolio. Do not claim that solar-plus-storage eliminates grid dependence; grid interconnection and backup grid supply remain necessary for most warehouse configurations.

*Legal Confirmation Required:* credit eligibility, the identity of the claiming entity (owner versus lessee versus operator), and transferability under the federal tax-credit provisions require tax counsel review before any client or investor representation is made.

**Questions to pose to clients:**

- Does your Scope 3 supplier data programme currently capture warehouse-level electricity source data from freight handlers?
- Are your distribution or storage facilities in regions where peak demand charges are a significant portion of the electricity bill?

---

# 7. Pending Changes That Shift the Calculus

### MONITORING

**Monitoring timeline:**
- December 12, 2024 Applicability dates: For dates of applicability, see Sec. Sec. 1.48-9(g), 1.48-13(f), 1.48-14(j), and 1.6418-5(j).: the US Treasury / IRS final regulations on energy property and the energy credit took effect.

FACT: "at construction must begin before January 1, 2025. Further, the IRA amendments included a special rule to allow cer" *Source: Federal Register, US Treasury / IRS final regulations. https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2024/12/12/2024-28190/definition-of-energy-property-and-rules-applicable-to-the-energy-credit

*Analytical inference:* the construction-commencement deadline referenced in this rule is a planning variable for any workspace considering a warehouse solar-plus-BESS investment intended to qualify under this credit regime; the specific applicability of this rule to a given project depends on when construction begins and is a matter for tax counsel review.

FACT: "Section 48 originally was enacted by section 2 of the Revenue Act of 1962, Public Law 87-834, 76 Stat. 960, 963 (October 16, 1962), to spur economic growth by encouraging investments in various capital projects across many industries including energy, transportation, and communications. Section 48 has been amended many times since its enactment, most recently by section 13102 of Public Law 117-169, 136 Stat. 1818 (August 16, 2022), commonly known as the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 (IRA)." *Source: Federal Register, US Treasury / IRS final regulations. https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2024/12/12/2024-28190/definition-of-energy-property-and-rules-applicable-to-the-energy-credit

*Analytical inference:* as CSRD enforcement reaches the first wave of large EU-based companies and ISSB S2 adoption expands in other jurisdictions, clients with Scope 3 supplier-data programmes will increasingly request warehouse-level electricity-source data from logistics partners; workspaces that have deployed metered on-site solar will be able to supply market-based Scope 2 figures rather than location-based grid-average figures. This regulatory pressure is a secondary commercial driver for the solar-plus-BESS investment case beyond direct energy cost savings.
